lesson_title: The Compass That Flinched: Electromagnetism and Faraday's Law
hook_text: For eleven years, physicists left magnets next to wires, waiting for electricity. Nothing. They were missing one word.
clip_script: 1820. A lecturer named Oersted switches on a current, and a compass on his bench FLINCHES. Switch off — it relaxes. Electricity was making magnetism, and the whole world took notes. So physicists asked the obvious follow-up: can magnetism make electricity? They put mighty magnets next to coils of wire and watched the meters. Nothing. For ELEVEN YEARS, nothing. Because everyone was missing one word: CHANGE. Faraday found it. Push the magnet toward the coil — current flows. Stop — it dies instantly, even with the magnet touching the coil. Pull away — current again, backwards. A resting magnet makes nothing; a MOVING one makes electricity every time, and the faster you move it, the more you get. More turns on the coil? Two hundred loops push two hundred times harder. One catch: the current you induce always fights you — shove a north pole in, the coil turns its own north face toward you and shoves back. You pay in effort; you get paid in electricity. Now scale it up: spinning coils, roaring turbines — that's every power station on Earth. Your phone is charging on Faraday's one word.
visual_style: A candle-lit 1820 lecture bench with a twitching compass; a montage of frustrated scientists and dead meters with years ticking past; then a magnet plunging into a coil with the meter leaping, ending on turbines spinning into a glowing city grid.
mood: Historical detective story — a decade-long mystery cracked by a single word.
pacing: Period-drama open, tense stalled middle, triumphant accelerating finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and own the law that lights the whole country.
